column5: taught tongue and awakened ear
column6: The commentary says the addressee will recite because God teaches him; Isaiah's speaker receives a trained tongue and a morning-awakened ear to hear like a disciple, joining divine instruction to receptive listening.

column5: words placed in the prophet's mouth
column6: God touches Jeremiah's mouth and says he has put his words there; this gives a direct prophetic scene for the commentary's promise that God will make the addressee recite.

column5: prophet speaks words placed in his mouth
column6: God promises to put his words in a prophet's mouth, who must speak all he is commanded; this frames recitation as received speech and accountable transmission.

column5: God teaches Moses what to say
column6: Moses protests that he is not eloquent, and God answers that he will be with his mouth and teach him what to speak; the promise locates successful speech in divine enabling.

column5: Spirit and word on the tongue
column6: David says the Lord's spirit speaks through him and God's word is on his tongue; this joins divine source and human utterance as the commentary does.

column5: spirit and words remain in mouths
column6: God's covenant promises that his spirit and words placed in the addressee's mouth will remain with him and his descendants; this adds enduring communal transmission to the promise of retained recitation.

column5: eating and inwardly receiving words
column6: Jeremiah says he found and ate God's words, which became joy to him; this gives an image of divine speech taken inward before it is carried outward.

column5: eat the scroll, then speak
column6: God tells Ezekiel to eat a scroll and then go speak to Israel; the sequence concretely joins receiving words inside with later public transmission, like the commentary's holding-then-releasing image.

column5: scroll enters the mouth and tastes sweet
column6: The scroll fills Ezekiel's stomach and tastes like honey in his mouth; it portrays the prophetic message as fully received rather than merely heard.

column5: take the words to heart and listen
column6: God tells Ezekiel to take all the words into his heart and hear them with his ears before speaking; this closely matches the commentary's inward retention of a received recitation.

column5: song put into Israel's mouths
column6: Moses must write and teach a song so it can be put into Israel's mouths; the text makes memorized utterance a divinely arranged witness, extending the commentary's promise beyond one listener.

column5: song not forgotten by descendants
column6: Moses says the song will not be forgotten from the mouths of Israel's descendants; unlike the individual prophetic promise, this makes preservation a multigenerational result.

column5: Hebrew qara, read aloud
column6: The Hebrew qaraʾ verb here means reading the Torah before all Israel; it is a cognate of the Arabic q-r-ʾ label in the commentary and places the shared reading-family word in public scriptural recitation.

column5: public Torah reading to all Israel
column6: Moses is instructed to read the law before the assembled people so they hear and learn; this gives the commentary's divinely enabled recitation a communal counterpart.

column5: covenant read, then followed
column6: Moses reads the covenant book aloud and Israel answers that they will do and heed it; the sequence shows listening to a recitation issuing in following it.

column5: Hebrew qara, read and expound
column6: The Hebrew qaraʾ reading verb occurs as the Torah is read; the cognate sense is specifically public scriptural reading, while the verse's explanation of the text adds interpretation to recitation.

column5: reading with explanation
column6: The Levites read God's law and give its sense so the people understand; this illuminates the commentary's distinction between reciting words and having their meaning made clear.

column5: Hebrew qara, Baruch reads the scroll
column6: The Hebrew qaraʾ verb describes Baruch reading Jeremiah's written words aloud; this is a cognate reading use, concretely tied to a message received from God and relayed by another voice.

column5: Baruch recites Jeremiah's words publicly
column6: Baruch reads the scroll before the people on a fast day; the mediated reading complements the commentary's image of a hearer following the reciter.

column5: scroll burned but its words answered
column6: After the king burns the scroll, the Lord's word comes to Jeremiah again; the episode gives a concrete case of human rejection failing to make the divine message disappear.

column5: scroll ordered to be written again
column6: God commands Jeremiah to take another scroll and write the former words again after Jehoiakim's burning; the repeated inscription supplies a narrative of preservation through renewed dictation.

column5: rewritten scroll with added words
column6: Baruch writes the words again from Jeremiah's dictation, with many similar words added; this shows transmission surviving destruction and growing through a new recitation.

column5: word from God's mouth fulfills its purpose
column6: God's word goes out from his mouth and accomplishes what he intends; beside the commentary's promise that recitation will not be lost, this emphasizes the efficacy of the source, not the hearer's memory alone.

column5: word endures after grass withers
column6: Isaiah contrasts withering grass and fading flowers with God's word standing forever; this meets the commentary's immediate move from pasture turned to refuse to the promise of a word that will not be dropped.

column5: words placed on the heart
column6: Israel must keep the commanded words on the heart; this offers a covenantal form of inward retention alongside the commentary's prophetic guarantee.

column5: teach and speak the words continually
column6: The words are to be taught to children and spoken at home and on the road; this turns inwardly retained teaching into repeated speech across generations.

column5: word near mouth and heart
column6: The command is very near, in the mouth and heart to be done; this links internal possession, spoken words, and action, rather than treating recitation as sound alone.

column5: law remains in the mouth and is meditated on
column6: The book of the law is not to depart from Joshua's mouth, and he is to meditate on it day and night; this describes sustained recitation and practice, while the surah makes retention a divine promise.

column5: word stored in the heart
column6: The psalmist says he has treasured God's word in his heart; this is a clear image of gathered words kept inwardly, though here the speaker describes his own devotional practice.

column5: not forgetting God's word
column6: The psalmist resolves not to forget God's word while delighting in the statutes; it concretizes the same result that the commentary attributes to God's recitation.

column5: not forgetting the precepts
column6: The speaker says God's precepts preserve his life and he will never forget them; this adds a received-word testimony in which memory sustains life.

column5: law written within the heart
column6: God promises a covenant with the law placed within and written on the people's hearts; this communal inward inscription develops the commentary's image of a word held inside before it is spoken.

column5: forgetting God means failing to keep commands
column6: Israel is warned not to forget the Lord by failing to keep his commandments; this clarifies the commentary's secondary sense of forgetting as abandonment, not only a lapse of memory.

column5: God will not forget Zion even if a mother might
column6: The passage imagines a mother forgetting her nursing child, then denies that God will forget Zion; it adds a maternal image to the commentary's claim that the giver of memory does not abandon what is entrusted.

column5: God does not forget the covenant
column6: God is merciful and will not abandon Israel or forget the covenant with the ancestors; this anchors retained revelation in divine fidelity to an earlier promise.

column5: God remembers covenant and acts
column6: God hears Israel's groaning, remembers the covenant with the ancestors, and turns toward the enslaved people; this shows remembrance as active fidelity, the ground the commentary gives for a preserved message.

column5: God chooses not to remember sins
column6: God says he blots out transgressions and will not remember sins; beside the surah's exception reserving memory to God's will, this shows divine non-remembrance as an act of mercy toward a different object.

column5: human life like grass
column6: The human being flourishes like field grass and disappears when the wind passes; this gives a scriptural form to the commentary's adjacent image of vegetation becoming refuse.

column5: steadfast love lasts beyond human life
column6: After describing human life as grass, the psalm says the Lord's steadfast love is everlasting; this places divine permanence beside the commentary's contrast between withered pasture and enduring word.

column5: the forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
column6: If a reaper forgets a sheaf, it must remain for the immigrant, orphan, and widow; unlike the commentary's abandoned camp refuse, the forgotten object becomes provision for the vulnerable, adding an ethical reversal.

column5: wishing to be an unregarded stillbirth
column6: Job wishes he had been like a hidden stillbirth that never saw light; this shares the birth-lament behind Mary's wish to have been forgotten, while Job's own suffering rather than childbirth frames the speech.

column5: Jeremiah curses the day of his birth
column6: Jeremiah wishes the day of his birth had not been blessed; this is a prophetic birth lament beside Mary's wish to die and become forgotten, but the two speakers and settings remain distinct.

column5: why was I born to see toil?
column6: Jeremiah asks why he came from the womb only to see sorrow; the question shares Mary's acute labor-time wish for erasure without making her scene the same story.

column5: grass and flower wither
column6: Isaiah says grass withers and flower fades; beside the surah's pasture becoming dark refuse before the promise of retention, it sharpens the contrast between transient vegetation and lasting divine speech.

column5: Spirit teaches and reminds
column6: The Paraclete will teach the disciples and remind them of everything Jesus said; this is the closest Christian formulation of received words retained by divine agency, while its addressees are the disciples collectively.

column5: Spirit teaches what to say
column6: The Holy Spirit will teach the disciples what they ought to say when brought before authorities; this parallels the future promise of divinely enabled speech in a specific trial setting.

column5: Father's Spirit speaks through disciples
column6: Jesus says the Spirit of the Father speaks in the disciples when they testify; the saying locates their words' source in God, like the commentary's account of recitation received rather than self-generated.

column5: words taught by the Spirit
column6: Paul contrasts Spirit-taught words with human wisdom; this makes the content and manner of speech dependent on divine teaching, adding an apostolic setting to the commentary's promise.

column5: prophets carried by the Holy Spirit
column6: Prophecy did not come by human will, but people spoke from God as they were carried by the Spirit; this gives a concise account of divine source and human utterance.

column5: Spirit writes on human hearts
column6: Paul calls the community a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God on hearts; this joins the commentary's inwardly held word to a Christian image of divine inscription.

column5: minds opened to understand Scripture
column6: The risen Jesus opens the disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures; this adds divine enabling of comprehension to the commentary's promise to make the addressee recite.

column5: Deuteronomy's word read as preached faith
column6: Paul quotes the word near mouth and heart from Deuteronomy and identifies it as the word of faith he proclaims; this Christian interpretation turns Torah's inward and spoken command into a preached confession.

column5: law written on minds and hearts
column6: The new-covenant quotation promises God's laws in minds and written on hearts; this develops inward retention as a covenantal gift, not merely a reader's discipline.

column5: doing rather than forgetting the heard word
column6: The person who looks into the law and perseveres is a doer, not a forgetful hearer; this gives a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that true reading becomes a life of obedience.

column5: word held fast and bearing fruit
column6: The good soil hears the word, holds it fast in an honest heart, and bears fruit with perseverance; it meets the commentary's agricultural setting with a distinct image of received speech retained until it yields action.

column5: eat the scroll
column6: The seer is told to eat the scroll, sweet in the mouth but bitter in the stomach; like Ezekiel and the commentary's inward-retention metaphor, the message is taken inside, while Revelation adds the cost of its contents.

column5: received words become renewed proclamation
column6: After eating the scroll, John is told to prophesy again about many peoples; the sequence makes inward reception the preparation for outward warning, close to the commentary's movement from not forgetting to reminding others.

column5: reading requires a guide
column6: Philip asks the Ethiopian whether he understands Isaiah's reading, and the man says he needs a guide; this gives a specific scene of recitation joined to teaching and interpretation.

column5: Scripture explained as good news
column6: Philip begins from the passage the Ethiopian is reading and tells him the good news about Jesus; this shows a received text being opened and transmitted to another listener.

column5: public reading, exhortation, teaching
column6: Timothy is charged to attend to public reading alongside exhortation and teaching; the Syriac reading tradition also gives a cognate form for the commentary's reading word.

column5: called from the womb
column6: Paul says God set him apart from his mother's womb and called him by grace; this joins the commentary's womb image to prophetic vocation, though Paul is describing his own apostolic call.

column5: revelation within followed by preaching
column6: God reveals his Son in Paul so that Paul may preach among the nations; this offers a distinct Christian sequence of inward reception and outward delivery.

column5: creation through the Word
column6: The opening says all things came to be through the Word; this complements the commentary's pairing of creation and divine teaching by locating creation in the one who is God's Word.

column5: Word makes the unseen God known
column6: The prologue says the only Son has made God known; read alongside its claim that creation came through the Word, it offers a Christian pairing of creator and revealer like the commentary's creator-teacher sequence.

column5: God speaks through prophets across times
column6: God spoke to the ancestors in many ways through the prophets; this places the surah's direct divine address within a wider scriptural pattern of mediated revelation.

column5: Mary's birth narrated without the lament
column6: Luke narrates Mary giving birth in Bethlehem, swaddling Jesus, and laying him in a manger, whereas the Qur'anic scene foregrounds her wish to be forgotten and God's consolation; the different framing matters without making a shared scene identical.

column5: king reads the law throughout life
column6: The king must read the law all his days, learn reverence, and keep its words; this supplies a sustained practice of reading beyond the single prophetic promise.

column5: study, practice, then teach
column6: Ezra sets his heart to study the law, do it, and teach it; this matches the commentary's reading-as-devotion and links inward learning to public instruction.

column5: Torah as creation's blueprint
column6: The midrash pictures God consulting Torah as a builder consults a plan before making the world; it gives a Jewish interpretive link between creation and revealed teaching like the commentary's creator-teacher pairing.

column5: scribe studies prophecy and speaks wisdom
column6: The scribe studies the law and prophets, seeks hidden meanings, and is filled with a spirit of understanding to pour out wise words; this adds a learned Jewish model of received instruction becoming speech.

column5: God governs speech and understanding
column6: The speaker asks God to grant fitting speech and says both people and their words are in God's hand; this extends divine agency from recitation to the speaker's very words.

column5: wisdom and spirit sent from above
column6: The passage asks who could know God's counsel unless God gave wisdom and sent a holy spirit from above; this frames understanding as a gift, beside the commentary's promise of divine teaching.

column5: Ezra dictates books by divine enablement
column6: After Jerusalem's destruction Ezra is commanded to write, and the books are dictated through him; this gives a Jewish apocalyptic scene of preserved revelation being restored through an enabled human speaker.

column5: forgetting one word of Torah as culpable
column6: The Mishnah treats negligent loss of a learned word as grave; beside the surah's promise that the prophet will not forget, it makes the contrast between human obligation and divinely secured retention explicit.

column5: repeated oral teaching as preservation
column6: The rabbinic account has Moses repeat Torah teaching through Aaron, the elders, and Israel; it explains communal retention through rehearsed transmission rather than a single prophetic promise.

column4: John Chrysostom, Homilies on John, on John 14:25-26
column5: Spirit's reminder as Christ's teaching retained
column6: Chrysostom reads Jesus' promise that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples in its immediate setting; this Christian interpretation stresses preservation of Jesus' words rather than an unrelated new message.

column5: eating the scroll as inward appropriation
column6: Jerome's discussion of Ezekiel's eaten scroll treats reception of prophetic words as something to take within before teaching; it supplies a Christian interpretive bridge for the commentary's held-then-released word.

column5: Syriac nšy-family word for forgotten
column6: The Syriac Peshitta uses a verb from the nšy family for the sparrow not being forgotten before God; that is a cognate of the Arabic n-s-y label, while the Greek New Testament has a different root, and the context makes divine remembering concrete.

column5: Syriac qeryānā, public reading
column6: The Peshitta's Syriac reading term qeryānā belongs to the same Semitic reading-word family as Arabic q-r-ʾ; here it names public reading joined to teaching, while the SBL Greek word is not a cognate.

column5: sealed teaching among disciples
column6: Isaiah commands that the testimony be bound up and the teaching sealed among his disciples; this gives a concrete preservation practice beside the commentary's promise that recited words will not be lost.

column5: written witness for the future
column6: God tells Isaiah to inscribe the message in a book for future days as an enduring witness; this connects the commentary's assurance of retained speech with written preservation across time.

column5: Moses' promised prophet identified with Jesus
column6: Peter quotes Moses' promise of a prophet like him and applies it to Jesus; this gives a Christian reading of the very Mosaic pattern in which God places words in a prophet's mouth.

column5: received tradition handed on
column6: Paul says he handed on what he had received about Jesus' death and resurrection; this makes the source-to-recipient-to-listener chain explicit, adding a communal transmission formula to the commentary's carrier-of-words image.

column5: vision written plainly for a reader
column6: The prophet must write the vision on tablets so a reader can run with it; this joins inscription, legibility, and transmission to the commentary's account of a received message following a recitation.

column5: Moses completes the written law
column6: Moses finishes writing the words of the law in a book; this adds a textual witness to the surah's claim that revelation continues in earlier pages.

column5: book placed beside the ark as witness
column6: The book of the law is placed beside the covenant ark to remain a witness; this gives the commentary's preserved word an archival setting and a continuing role beyond its first hearers.

column5: sealed book preserved for the end
column6: Daniel is told to shut and seal the book until the time of the end; this gives a specific apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's references to a hidden book and protected revelation.

column5: God forms the inward parts in the womb
column6: The psalmist says God formed him and knit him together in his mother's womb; the passage's own creation scene gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's explicitly metaphorical womb image.

column5: womb formation and days written in a book
column6: The psalm joins God's sight of the unformed body with days written in a book; this uniquely meets the commentary's conjunction of womb-held life and a word securely kept by God.

column5: book of remembrance for those who fear God
column6: A book of remembrance is written before God for those who fear him and remember his name; this makes the commentary's divine knowledge and retained remembrance a recorded communal witness.

column5: books opened before the heavenly court
column6: Daniel sees books opened for judgment; this adds a scene of deeds preserved in divine records beside the commentary's claim that what is public and hidden remains within God's knowledge.

column5: forgetting God pictured as neglect
column6: The prophet asks whether a bride can forget her ornaments, then says Israel has forgotten God; this gives the commentary's secondary sense of forgetting as abandonment a concrete relational image.

column5: Moses, prophets, and psalms read as fulfilled in Jesus
column6: Jesus says that what is written in the Law of Moses, Prophets, and Psalms must be fulfilled; this Christian account of continuity with earlier scriptures belongs beside the commentary's claim that the recited message is also present in the earlier pages.

column5: entrust what was heard to future teachers
column6: Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others; this makes the retained message a deliberate chain of transmission, extending the commentary's inward reception and outward reminder.

column5: books opened and deeds judged
column6: The dead are judged from what is written in opened books; this gives a Christian apocalyptic instance of divine knowledge preserved as a record, like the commentary's connection between hidden deeds and God's book.

column5: Torah transmission from Moses onward
column6: The Mishnah traces Torah from Moses through Joshua, elders, prophets, and later teachers; it presents revelation as a handed-on chain, adding a Jewish communal model beside the commentary's direct divine address to one recipient.

column5: Wisdom identified with Moses' Torah
column6: Sirach identifies personified Wisdom with the book of the covenant and the law commanded by Moses; this gives a Jewish interpretive bridge between divine teaching and the earlier Mosaic pages named in the surah.

column5: Enoch reads heavenly tablets and records them
column6: Enoch reads the heavenly tablets, understands them, and records what they contain; this adds a Jewish apocalyptic image of revelation preserved in a celestial book and passed on in writing.

column5: prophets and apostolic memoirs read in assembly
column6: Justin describes public reading of prophetic and apostolic writings followed by an exhortation to imitate them; this connects the commentary's recitation, listening, and lived devotion with early Christian worship.

column5: Mary's birth in the cave with a midwife
column6: The apocryphal narrative places Jesus' birth in a cave and has Joseph summon a midwife, whereas the Qur'anic Mary scene foregrounds solitary labor, distress, and a wish to be forgotten; the distinct birth framing adds an early Christian account beside the Qur'anic one.
